observations.text: In 2Chr 29:31, todah (thank offerings) co-occurs with M22 (glory-related 'said'), M23/M72 (consecrated), M44 (assembly), M09/M34 (willing), M47 (heart), M36 (burnt offerings). observations.text: Across its full occurrence list H8426 clusters into three recurring realizations of one lexeme: (1) the concrete thank-offering sacrifice (Lev.7.12 x2, Lev.7.13, Lev.7.15, Lev.22.29, Ps.50.14, Ps.50.23, Ps.107.22, Ps.116.17, Amos.4.5, Jonah.2.9, 2Chr.29.31 x2, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11), (2) the vocal/manner accompaniment of praise, 'with/in thanksgiving' (Ps.69.30, Ps.26.7, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Isa.51.3), and (3) the institutional thanksgiving choir/procession/company (Neh.12.27, Neh.12.31, Neh.12.38, Neh.12.40, Ps.42.4). A fourth, rarer sense realizes it as verbal confession (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11). This is a single strong showing internally the full sense-range attributed to the subgroup label (hymn, choir, offering) without needing a second member strong to supply any of these senses.

disposition.reason: a lexical note: the three uses of H8426 across its occurrences, with no inner-being content

observations.text: Since H8426 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, there is no second lexeme to compare it against directly; the meaningful cross-comparison available is internal -- between H8426's own sacrificial/cultic-object occurrences (e.g. Lev.7.12-15, Lev.22.29, 2Chr.29.31, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11, Amos.4.5) versus its choir/procession-as-institution occurrences (Neh.12.27-40, Ps.42.4) versus its purely adverbial/manner occurrences ('with thanksgiving', e.g. Ps.69.30, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Ps.26.7). These three groupings do not overlap grammatically: the sacrificial sense is always the head noun or a construct-genitive qualifier of an offering-word (zebach, shelamim), the choir sense functions as a collective-body noun (subject or object of appointment/movement verbs), and the manner sense is marked by a preposition (b-) modifying a separate main verb of praise. No morphological distinction (all occurrences are the same feminine noun stem, singular or plural absolute/construct) drives this three-way split -- it is purely syntactic/contextual, meaning the noun's referent is disambiguated entirely by its syntactic role in each verse rather than by any inflectional change.

disposition.reason: a lexical note: an internal comparison of H8426's uses, with no inner-being content

observations.text: Todah takes hold rightly under conditions of a willing heart (2Chr.29.31, 'all who were of a willing heart') and right ordering of one's way of life (Ps.50.23, 'to one who orders his way rightly'); it operates rightly when accompanied by genuine acknowledgment rather than mere ritual performance.

The human-to-God movement of todah requires an inner posture of humility and right-ordering ('to one who orders his way rightly,' Ps.50.23), willingness ('willing heart,' 2Chr.29.31), and honest acknowledgment (confession, Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11) rather than mere external ritual performance.

2Chr.29.31 shows that genuine extension of todah is accompanied by consecration ('you have now consecrated yourselves to the Lord') and a willing heart, indicating that inner conditions of dedication and voluntary devotion in the giver (here, the assembly/nation) accompany the sincere bringing of thank-offerings.

2Chr.29.31 shows the assembly had first to consecrate themselves before bringing thank offerings, indicating a person must have first undergone consecration/dedication to the Lord before rightly extending todah.

Todah ends where a different sacrificial category begins: it is explicitly distinguished from the burnt offering (2Chr.29.31, 'brought sacrifices and thank offerings...brought burnt offerings') and from the peace offering more generally, being a specific sub-type marked by gratitude/acknowledgment rather than full dedication (burnt offering) or general fellowship (peace offering).

disposition.reason: a lexical note: where todah ends as a sacrificial category, with no inner-being content

observations.text: Fear of a people or a person falls on others.
observations.meaning: Fear of a people or a person falls on others. "many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them"; officials "helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them". Of Nebuchadnezzar: "because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed". Of Ephraim: "When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel, but he incurred guilt through Baal and died". Of the king of Babylon: "Is this the man who made the earth tremble"

observations.text: Dread laid on peoples and creatures, and what it led to.
observations.meaning: Meaning: dread is laid by God, or falls because of his people, and the verses say what it did: the cities did not pursue. Implies: in Rahab, the dread came by hearing, melted heart and spirit, and ends in a confession of God. In Moab, the same dread ends in hiring a curse. Psa 9:20 asks for fear so that the nations know what they are.

observations.text: What inspires dread in creatures, in visions, and in love.
observations.meaning: Setting: Job 39–41 is God's own speech about the creatures he made. Meaning: the dread word describes the thing feared. Implies: in the Song, the same word describes the beloved's beauty.

observations.text: Fear holds back from an act: the young man "did not draw his sword, for he was afraid"; the armor-bearer "would not, for he feared greatly"; "the people feared the oath"
observations.meaning: Fear holds back from an act: the young man "did not draw his sword, for he was afraid"; the armor-bearer "would not, for he feared greatly"; "the people feared the oath"

observations.text: Anger and jealousy named together.
observations.meaning: jealousy is named beside the anger in the setting of other gods and broken covenant.

observations.text: "I said I would pour out my wrath … But I acted for the sake of my name."
observations.meaning: each round has rebellion, the wrath resolved on, then the wrath withheld "for the sake of my name … in the sight of the nations".

observations.text: The hard heart named as the cause.
observations.meaning: both verses put the heart first and the anger after it. In Deuteronomy the verb is "smoke" (ʿāšan).

observations.text: The smoke word.
observations.meaning: ʿāšan is the word for Sinai smoking when God came down, and for mountains smoking at his touch. In Psa 74:1 and Deu 29:20 it is the word for his anger toward his people. In Psa 80:4 the ESV renders it "be angry", and it is against "your people's prayers".

observations.text: God's act on the heart is named beside the person's "would not": "the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go" (Exo 10:27); "Sihon the king of Heshbon would not let us pass by him, for the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that he might give him into your hand" (Deu 2:30).
observations.meaning: The verses give both the hardened heart or spirit and the unwillingness, and in Deu 2:30 the purpose; they do not explain more.

observations.text: The willing heart and spirit (nādîb): "Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring" (Exo 35:5); "All who were of a willing heart brought" (Exo 35:22), after "everyone whose heart stirred him" (35:21); after consecration, "all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings" (2Ch 29:31); with God's plan for the temple, "with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill" (1Ch 28:21); and asked of God, "uphold me with a willing spirit" (Psa 51:12).
observations.meaning: Willingness rises in the person, the heart stirring them to give, and is also upheld by God in prayer; a plan given by God and the willing who carry it out stand together.

observations.text: What God offered and was refused was good: the land, "Yet you would not go up, but rebelled" (Deu 1:26); rest, "This is rest; give rest to the weary," "yet they would not hear" (Isa 28:12); "In returning and rest you shall be saved" "But you were unwilling" (Isa 30:15), with their own plan, "We will flee upon horses" (30:16); "children unwilling to hear the instruction of the Lord" (Isa 30:9); "Israel would not submit to me" (Psa 81:11), "So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels" (81:12); "would have none of my reproof" (Pro 1:25), "would have none of my counsel" (Pro 1:30); "whose law they would not obey" (Isa 42:24); "will not listen to me" (Lev 26:21); "not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart" (Eze 3:7); "they rebelled against me and were not willing to listen to me" (Eze 20:8). Once the will is invited with if: "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land" (Isa 1:19).
observations.meaning: Refusing God is refusing his good (land, rest, counsel); the refusal is set beside the people's own plans and counsels, and beside a hard or stubborn heart.

observations.text: God's will, and the reason each verse gives: after intercession, "the Lord listened to me that time also. The Lord was unwilling to destroy you" (Deu 10:10); for a promise, "the Lord was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant" (2Ki 8:19), "because of the covenant that he had made with David" (2Ch 21:7); in grace, "the Lord was gracious to them and had compassion on them" "and would not destroy them" (2Ki 13:23); out of love, "the Lord your God would not listen to Balaam" "because the Lord your God loved you" (Deu 23:5; Jos 24:10). And against: "the Lord will not be willing to forgive him" (Deu 29:20), of the one who "blesses himself in his heart" (29:19); "he filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the Lord would not pardon" (2Ki 24:4).
observations.meaning: God's not willing to destroy rests on intercession, promise, covenant, compassion and love; his not willing to forgive rests on a self-blessing stubborn heart and on innocent blood.

observations.text: The Hebrew will (ʾabâ) answers what another puts before it: a request, "Please let us pass through your land," and the king of Moab "would not consent" (Judg 11:17); "Let my servants go with your servants in the ships," but "Jehoshaphat was not willing" (1Ki 22:49); after days of pressing, "the man would not spend the night" (Judg 19:10); Absalom "pressed him, but he would not go" (2Sa 13:25); "Joab would not come" (2Sa 14:29). A plan allows for another's will: "Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me" (Gen 24:5), with a way out, "if the woman is not willing to follow you, then you will be free from this oath" (Gen 24:8). After defeat, "the Syrians were not willing to save the Ammonites anymore" (1Ch 19:19).
observations.meaning: In these narratives the will is seldom shown starting on its own: it is the inner yes or no to what someone else asks, presses or offers, and another person's plan has to reckon with it.

observations.text: A refusal that keeps faith: "the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the Lord" (1Sa 22:17); David, "I would not put out my hand against the Lord's anointed" (1Sa 26:23); David longed for the water of Bethlehem, "But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord" (2Sa 23:16), "Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?" (2Sa 23:17; 1Ch 11:18-19). The faithful refuse enticement and demand: "you shall not yield to him or listen to him" (Deu 13:8); "if sinners entice you, do not consent" (Pro 1:10); "Do not listen or consent" (1Ki 20:8).
observations.meaning: The will's no can be faithfulness: to God's anointed and priests, to the lives of others, and against enticement, even from one's own household or friend.

observations.text: A refusal can cost the one who makes it: warned to turn aside, "Asahel would not turn aside from following him" (2Sa 2:21), and he died; "if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife," she goes to the elders at the gate (Deu 25:7), and he is publicly shamed (25:9-10); Saul and the people "spared Agag and the best of the sheep" and "would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction" (1Sa 15:9).
observations.meaning: The will's no carries consequences for the one who refuses: death, public shame, or God's rejection. Saul's refusal was selective: what they valued they kept.

observations.text: A refusal from inside a feeling: fear, "David was afraid of the Lord that day" and "was not willing to take the ark of the Lord into the city of David" (2Sa 6:9-10), until "it was told King David, The Lord has blessed the household of Obed-edom" (6:12); grief, the elders came "to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them" (2Sa 12:17); jealousy, "He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts" (Pro 6:35).
observations.meaning: Fear, grief and jealousy hold the will in a no; what a person then hears can change what they are willing to do.

observations.text: The same verb names a violent refusal: Amnon "would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her" (2Sa 13:14), and again "he would not listen to her" when she pleaded not to be sent away (2Sa 13:16); at Gibeah "the men would not listen to him" (Judg 19:25); "the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers" when asked to give up the guilty (Judg 20:13).
observations.meaning: Here the will's no is the stronger shutting out the plea of the weaker, or a people shielding evil against the call to purge it.

observations.text: Among the creatures God sets beyond a man's control: "Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger?" (Job 39:9).
observations.meaning: The will word is used of a beast that will not serve a man, in God's questions to Job.

observations.text: The Aramaic will word (ṣəbâ) sets an absolute human will under the Most High: of Nebuchadnezzar, "Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive" (Dan 5:19); what he was to learn, "the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will" (Dan 4:17, 25, 32; 5:21); and "he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand" (Dan 4:35). Daniel uses the same word: "I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast" (Dan 7:19).
observations.meaning: A king's will made absolute is brought down so that he knows whose will rules; the next verse names what happened in him, "his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened" (Dan 5:20).

claims.text: No verse read makes the spirit the subject of "to sin". But the spirit is morally judged: haughty before a fall (Pro 16:18), "spirit was not faithful" (Psa 78:8), hardened by God (Deu 2:30), needing to be made "right" (Psa 51:10), with or without deceit (Psa 32:2), defiled with the body (2Co 7:1). The part Scripture judges most is the heart (D §3.4, §9.2, §11.1–3; C §9.2). The original itself listed Pro 16:18 and Deu 2:30, then set them aside

blocks.section: The heart decides and is moved
blocks.text:
## The heart decides and is moved

- "Daniel resolved [set on his heart] that he would not defile himself with the king's food" (Daniel 1:8).
- "Each one must give as he has decided in his heart" (2 Corinthians 9:7).
- David had it "in my heart to build a house" (1 Chronicles 28:2).
- When the tabernacle was built, "everyone whose heart stirred him" brought an offering (Exodus 35:21).
- The heart's purposes run deep: "The purpose in a man's heart is like deep water, but a man of understanding will draw it out" (Proverbs 20:5).
- The heart can be awake when the body is not, and still not move it: "I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking" (Song of Songs 5:2). She delayed for her comfort, "I had put off my garment; how could I put it on?" (5:3), though "my heart was thrilled within me" (5:4). When she opened, "my beloved had turned and gone" (5:6; 10.6).

The verses on willing name the heart beside the will again and again (10.7, *Willing*).
- **A willing heart gives.** "All who were of a willing heart brought" (Exodus 35:22). After consecration, "all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings" (2 Chronicles 29:31).
- **A hardened heart will not.** "But the Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go" (Exodus 10:27). Of Sihon: "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deuteronomy 2:30).
- **A stubborn heart will not listen.** "the house of Israel will not be willing to listen to you, for they are not willing to listen to me: because all the house of Israel have a hard forehead and a stubborn heart" (Ezekiel 3:7). And when Israel would not submit, "I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels" (Psalm 81:12).
- **A melted heart will not go.** "Yet you would not go up" (Deuteronomy 1:26), because "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" (1:28).
- **A heart that blesses itself.** "I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart" (Deuteronomy 29:19). Of that man, "The Lord will not be willing to forgive him" (29:20).
- **A heart lifted up.** Nebuchadnezzar's will was absolute, "Whom he would, he killed" (Daniel 5:19), "But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down" (5:20). His son "knew all this", and Daniel says to him, "you … have not humbled your heart" (5:22).
  - The words of that heart are given earlier: "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?" "While the words were still in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven" (Daniel 4:30–31). He had been told that his kingdom would be confirmed "from the time that you know that Heaven rules" (4:26). I read the boast as that heart speaking.
- **A heart not right, wanting power.** Simon offered money: "Give me this power also". Peter: "your heart is not right before God … pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you" (Acts 8:19, 21–22).
- **Hearts inclined by kinship.** Abimelech asked the men of Shechem to choose one ruler over seventy, "Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh", and "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3).
- **No one comes near of his own heart.** Of the ruler to come: "I will make him draw near, and he shall approach me, for who would dare of himself to approach me? declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 30:21). The words rendered "dare of himself" carry the word for the heart. The nearness is God's doing.

## The heart and anger

Anger is mostly described by what it does: a face falls, a hand strikes, a king gives an order. When the verses do name the heart in an anger, they give it a part to play, and the part differs from verse to verse. In the narratives, the angry person's own heart is rarely named. In Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes it is named often, and there anger is something to be held, kept or removed.

The heart is named **just before** the anger, in the state it was in when the anger came.
- Haman "went out that day joyful and glad of heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath against Mordecai" (Esther 5:9).
- "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (2 Chronicles 26:16). The Hebrew has *his heart was lifted up*. Three verses later Uzziah's anger at the priests breaks out with leprosy (26:19).

The heart is where anger is **kept and planned**.
- "The godless in heart cherish anger" (Job 36:13).
- "With perverted heart devises evil, continually sowing discord" (Proverbs 6:14).
- Esau "hated Jacob because of the blessing", and "Esau said to himself" (in his heart), "then I will kill my brother Jacob" (Genesis 27:41).

But the heart is also where anger is **taken to counsel**. Nehemiah was "very angry" at the outcry of the poor, and "I took counsel with myself, and I brought charges against the nobles" (Nehemiah 5:6–7). The Hebrew is *my heart took counsel*. The anger went into the heart and came out as a charge brought in the open.

It can **rage against God**. "When a man's folly brings his way to ruin, his heart rages against the Lord" (Proverbs 19:3).

It **carries vexation**, and can be cleared of it. "All his days are full of sorrow, and his work is a vexation. Even in the night his heart does not rest" (Ecclesiastes 2:23). "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (7:3). "Remove vexation from your heart, and put away pain from your body" (11:10).

It is **what must not faint** before another's anger. When the kings came against Jerusalem, "the heart of Ahaz and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind" (Isaiah 7:2). The word to Ahaz was: "Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin" (7:4).

The angry can **read another's heart wrongly**. Eliab, angry at David on the battlefield: "I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle" (1 Samuel 17:28). The chapter shows David was sent by his father with food (17:17–18, 20).

Under God's anger, the verses give the heart several roles, each in its own verses.
- **The heart that provokes it.** "And the Lord was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the Lord" (1 Kings 11:9). "Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah" (Psalm 95:8). "They made their hearts diamond-hard lest they should hear the law … Therefore great anger came from the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 7:12). "Because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath" (Romans 2:5).
- **The heart that turns it.** "Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the Lord, the God of Israel, in order that his fierce anger may turn away from us" (2 Chronicles 29:10). "But Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart … so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them" (2 Chronicles 32:26). Josiah was heard "because your heart was penitent" (2 Kings 22:19).
- **The heart that is called to be torn, or cut.** "Return to me with all your heart … and rend your hearts and not your garments" (Joel 2:12–13). "Circumcise yourselves to the Lord; remove the foreskin of your hearts … lest my wrath go forth like fire" (Jeremiah 4:4).
- **The heart that does not take it in.** "It set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25).
- **The heart that rejoices** when God's anger acts for it: "You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice … and the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall show his indignation against his enemies" (Isaiah 66:14).

In two places the heart named is the other person's. Jesus "looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5). And at Stephen's speech, "when they heard these things they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him" (Acts 7:54). The Greek of "enraged" is *sawn through in their hearts*: the word reached the heart before the stones were thrown.

God's own heart is named with his anger too. That is set out in 10.13 (Hosea 11:8; Jeremiah 23:20; Isaiah 63:4).

## The human spirit

What does a person's own spirit do, and what happens to it?

**It is troubled and anxious.** Pharaoh's "spirit was troubled" by his dreams (Genesis 41:8). Daniel: "my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me" (Daniel 7:15). Jesus was "troubled in his spirit" (John 13:21). Paul's "spirit was provoked within him" at the idols of Athens (Acts 17:16).

**It is crushed, and it faints.** "By sorrow of heart the spirit is crushed" (Proverbs 15:13). "A man's spirit will endure sickness, but a crushed spirit who can bear?" (Proverbs 18:14). "My spirit faints within me" (Psalm 143:4). Israel "did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery" (Exodus 6:9). A broken spirit can keep a person from even hearing good news. Job: "My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me" (Job 17:1).

**It revives, with food, drink and good news.** After three days without food, the Egyptian servant was given food, "and when he had eaten, his spirit revived" (1 Samuel 30:12). Samson drank, and "his spirit returned, and he revived" (Judges 15:19). When Jacob heard that Joseph was alive and saw the wagons, "the spirit of their father Jacob revived" (Genesis 45:27). In each case, food or drink came first.

**It knows.** "It is the spirit in man, the breath of the Almighty, that makes him understand" (Job 32:8). "Who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him?" (1 Corinthians 2:11). The spirit is where a person knows themselves. Jesus "perceiv[ed] in his spirit" what others were thinking (Mark 2:8).

**It is lowly or proud, and it is judged.** "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The next verse chooses the company: "It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud" (16:19). "One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor" (Proverbs 29:23). "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). The verse places the poverty in the spirit, not in what a person has, and the next blessing is on "those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (5:4). God dwells "with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). God looks to "he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2). Israel was "a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). The psalm's blessed man is "the one whose transgression is forgiven" (Psalm 32:1), the man "against whom the Lord counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit" (32:2). The no-deceit stands beside his confession: "I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity" (32:5). David prays for "a right spirit" (Psalm 51:10). Paul calls for cleansing "from every defilement of body and spirit" (2 Corinthians 7:1). And "the Lord weighs the spirit" (Proverbs 16:2).

This matters because it is often said that the human spirit never sins. It is true that I found no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin". But the spirit is certainly judged. It is proud or lowly, faithful or unfaithful, deceitful or clean, and it needs renewing.

**It is ruled, or it runs loose.** "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). "A man without self-control is like a city broken into and left without walls" (Proverbs 25:28). Self-control is the rule of one's own spirit. Without it, a person is a city with no walls. Anger and the spirit are often named together: "Be not quick in your spirit to become angry" (Ecclesiastes 7:9). And a prophet carrying God's word could say, "I went in bitterness in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the Lord being strong upon me" (Ezekiel 3:14). Chapter 10.1 follows how anger rises and is governed, and 10.13 gives the full account of anger.

**It is gentle, and it is under the person.** "restore him in a spirit of gentleness" (Galatians 6:1). "Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love in a spirit of gentleness?" (1 Corinthians 4:21). "a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1 Peter 3:4). "the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:32–33): the one who speaks governs what moves in him. And every spirit has one Father: "Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?" (Hebrews 12:9). Humility is in 10.14.

**In anger it is held back, heated, pressed and embittered.** The wisdom sayings speak of the spirit in an anger as something kept cool or let run: "the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit" (Ecclesiastes 7:8), and "he who has a cool spirit is a man of understanding" (Proverbs 17:27). "He who has a hasty temper exalts folly" (Proverbs 14:29) is literally short of spirit. In the accounts, the spirit is named in other ways.
- **Provoked:** Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16). What followed was reasoning: "So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews" (17:17).
- **Pressed until it speaks:** Elihu "burned with anger" (Job 32:2), waited, and then said, "the spirit within me constrains me" (32:18), and "I must speak, that I may find relief" (32:20).
- **Embittered, with the lips rash:** at Meribah "they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips" (Psalm 106:33). The verse does not say whether the spirit is Moses' or God's.
- **Receiving God's anger:** "the arrows of the Almighty are in me; my spirit drinks their poison" (Job 6:4).
- **What would faint,** and so is the reason God's anger is held back: "For I will not contend forever, nor will I always be angry; for the spirit would grow faint before me, and the breath of life that I made" (Isaiah 57:16). Moses pleaded on the same ground: "O God, the God of the spirits of all flesh, shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?" (Numbers 16:22).

**It is stirred, and it is hardened.** "The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia" (Ezra 1:1). The returning exiles were "everyone whose spirit God had stirred" (Ezra 1:5). Not everyone went; the stirred ones rose. Haggai shows what came before the stirring. The people "obeyed the voice of the Lord … And the people feared the Lord", and they were told "I am with you". Then "the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel … and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and worked on the house" (Haggai 1:12–14). The same chapter had them sowing much and harvesting little, clothed and not warm (1:6; 10.6). The spirit is stirred toward destroying too: "the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria" after his people "broke faith" (1 Chronicles 5:25–26), and "the spirit of the kings of the Medes" against Babylon (Jeremiah 51:11). 13.1 (*Stirring*) gathers what the verses say of God in this. And of Sihon: "the Lord your God hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate" (Deuteronomy 2:30), the same verse saying that he "would not let us pass by him". Nebuchadnezzar's spirit hardened itself with his pride: "when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down" (Daniel 5:20).

**It is willing.** "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Matthew 26:41). At the tabernacle, "everyone whose spirit moved him" came and brought (Exodus 35:21), and the next verse calls them "of a willing heart" (35:22). David asks for a willing spirit in the same prayer as a clean heart, a right spirit and God's Holy Spirit: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me … take not your Holy Spirit from me … uphold me with a willing spirit" (Psalm 51:10–12). The verse does not say whose spirit the willing spirit is. Verse 10 has "a right spirit within me" and verse 11 "your Holy Spirit", but verse 12 has neither "my" nor "your". What it says is that the willing spirit is asked of God, and that God upholds it. 10.7 (*Willing*) gives the account. Caleb "has a different spirit and has followed me fully" (Numbers 14:24).

**It is present where the body is not.** "Though absent in body, I am present in spirit" (1 Corinthians 5:3; Colossians 2:5).

The verbs in these verses are many: the spirit is moved, stirred, fervent ("fervent in spirit", Romans 12:11), willing, crushed, revived and ruled.

The human spirit is spoken of as kept alive by God. Job: "You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit" (Job 10:12). Hezekiah, recovered: "in all these is the life of my spirit" (Isaiah 38:16; Chapter 2).

blocks.section: Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find
blocks.text:
## Lines that are often drawn, but that I cannot find

Several confident distinctions are often taught. When I read the verses in their places, they did not hold up. Here they are, one by one.

**"The soul sins; the human spirit never does."** It is true that "the soul who sins shall die" (Ezekiel 18:4), but there the soul means the *person*, the one who answers for the sin. And while I find no verse where "the spirit" is the subject of the verb "to sin", the spirit is plainly judged. It is "haughty" before a fall (Proverbs 16:18). It was "not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). It is hardened (Deuteronomy 2:30). It needs to be made "right" (Psalm 51:10). It has or lacks "deceit" (Psalm 32:2). It needs cleansing from "defilement" (2 Corinthians 7:1). If Scripture has a *moral centre*, it is the heart (Chapter 12). The spirit stands beside it, not above it.

**"Animals have souls but not spirits."** The animals are "living creatures", the same phrase as the man in Genesis 2:7. But they also have "the breath of life". The flood came on "all flesh in which is the breath of life" (Genesis 6:17; 7:15), and there the word is *rûaḥ*. "They all have the same breath" (Ecclesiastes 3:19). There is "the spirit of the beast" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). "When you take away their breath, they die" (Psalm 104:29). What marks the man in Genesis 2:7 is not that he has breath and they do not. It is that **God himself breathed it into him**.

**"The soul faces the self; the spirit faces God."** The soul is the part that thirsts for God, lifts itself to God, waits for him and blesses him (Chapter 5). The spirit is anxious, provoked, hot-tempered and crushed (Chapter 6). Each faces both ways.

**"The soul goes to Sheol; the spirit goes to God."** The verses usually cited speak of the soul being *delivered from* Sheol ("you will not abandon my soul to Sheol", Psalm 16:10; "you have brought up my soul from Sheol", Psalm 30:3). Psalm 30:3 is about a living person rescued from death. Peter reads Psalm 16:10 of Christ, "not abandoned to Hades" (Acts 2:31). Neither sends the soul one way and the spirit another, and the verses that name Sheol or Hades speak of the soul and never of the spirit. And Ecclesiastes leaves the spirit's destination as a question: "Who knows whether the spirit of man goes upward?" (Ecclesiastes 3:21). See Chapter 2.

**"Spirit first, soul second, body third."** Scripture does not rank the inner words. It lists them in different orders for different purposes (Chapter 3). It gives God a soul as readily as a spirit: "my soul shall not abhor you" (Leviticus 26:11), "my soul delights" (Isaiah 42:1). It brings a dead child's life back as soul ("the life of the child came into him again", 1 Kings 17:22) as readily as spirit ("her spirit returned", Luke 8:55).

## How a feeling rises

Very often, something is seen or heard first.
- "The men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). They had just heard of it.
- "I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words" (Nehemiah 5:6).
- "When Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow down or pay homage to him, Haman was filled with fury" (Esther 3:5).
- Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16).

What is perceived may not even be true. Potiphar heard his wife's story, "his anger was kindled", and Joseph went to prison (Genesis 39:19–20). The officials "were enraged at Jeremiah" over a charge he had just called "a lie" (Jeremiah 37:14–15). The feeling acts on what it believes it has seen.

Anger often rises where a will is blocked:
- Balaam beats his donkey, and says why: "Because you have made a fool of me" (Numbers 22:29).
- Naaman: "Naaman was angry and went away, saying, 'Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me'" (2 Kings 5:11).
- Nebuchadnezzar is refused, and "the expression of his face was changed" (Daniel 3:19).

It rises where a heart that was lifted up is checked. Uzziah "when he was strong, he grew proud" (2 Chronicles 26:16). When the priests withstood him, "Uzziah was angry" (26:19). The king's anger burned when "the heart of the king was merry with wine" and his queen refused him (Esther 1:10–12). Chapter 11 follows this threshold further.

And anger rises on behalf of someone else. Jonathan "rose from the table in fierce anger … for he was grieved for David" (1 Samuel 20:34). When Jesus saw the children turned away, "he was indignant" (Mark 10:14).

Before the king's merry heart gave its command, the feast had set every guest free: "There is no compulsion", "to do as each man desired" (Esther 1:8, 10).

## Where it turns

A feeling can turn back on the one who has it. "You who tear yourself in your anger" (Job 18:4). Joseph forbids it: "do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here" (Genesis 45:5). Jonah, angry at God's mercy, asks to die: "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" (Jonah 4:9).

A feeling can even kill the one who has it. "Surely vexation kills the fool, and jealousy slays the simple" (Job 5:2). Chapter 2 sets this beside the other ways that end in death.

A feeling can be about life itself. Job: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul" (Job 10:1). Under the curse, life itself is held in dread: "Night and day you shall be in dread and have no assurance of your life" (Deuteronomy 28:66). And joy can fill a life so that its days are not counted: "God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart" (Ecclesiastes 5:20). Chapter 2 ("Life weighed") gives the account. Feeling also reaches toward a life that is threatened. Before Solomon, the true mother is known by it: "because her heart yearned for her son" (1 Kings 3:26). And the man brought back from the pit "sees his face with a shout of joy" (Job 33:26).

It can heat a person inside. "Fret not yourself" in Psalm 37 is literally *do not heat yourself*: "Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil" (Psalm 37:8). The psalm puts other movements in place of the heat: "Trust in the Lord … Commit your way to the Lord … Be still before the Lord and wait patiently for him" (37:3, 5, 7).

Anger can pass into another feeling. David was angry when God struck Uzzah, and then "David was afraid of the Lord that day" (2 Samuel 6:8–9). And it can be held together with grief. Jesus "looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5). His anger and his grief have the same object, and the next thing he does is heal.

Grief at a death takes more than one form:
- David fasted while his child lived, and rose when he died: "But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again?" (2 Samuel 12:23).
- Later, "the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead" (2 Samuel 13:39).
- Jeremiah turns the weeping elsewhere: "Weep not for him who is dead, nor grieve for him, but weep bitterly for him who goes away" (Jeremiah 22:10).
- Mary, at Jesus' feet: "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died" (John 11:32).

A feeling can hold the will in place (10.7, *Willing*).
- **Fear holds it.** After Uzzah, "David was not willing to take the ark of the Lord into the city of David" (2 Samuel 6:10). It was moved again by what he heard: "The Lord has blessed the household of Obed-edom," and he "brought up the ark of God … with rejoicing" (6:12).
- **Grief holds it.** While the child lived, "the elders of his house stood beside him, to raise him from the ground, but he would not, nor did he eat food with them" (2 Samuel 12:17).
- **Jealousy holds it.** "He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts" (Proverbs 6:35).

A groan can be a waiting. "We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). "For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling" (2 Corinthians 5:2). Chapter 2 ("The body raised") gives what is waited for.

Joy can be turned from one ground to another. "The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, 'Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name!'" Jesus did not take back the authority, but moved their joy: "Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven" (Luke 10:17, 20). "In that same hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit" (10:21; 13.3).

blocks.section: Delight > When delight is only the measure
blocks.text:
### When delight is only the measure

In many verses a delight word does not name the act the verse is about. It measures or qualifies another act, and the verse is placed with that act. In these verses delight is only the measure:

| Verse | The act the verse is about | Where |
|---|---|---|
| "they delight to draw near to God" (Isaiah 58:2) | seeking God daily, as if righteous, beside oppression | 10.7 |
| "they take no pleasure in it" (Jeremiah 6:10) | ears that cannot listen; the word scorned | 10.2 |
| "We do not desire the knowledge of your ways" (Job 21:14) | telling God to depart, and reckoning prayer by profit | 10.9 |
| "He did not delight in blessing" (Psalm 109:17) | cursing, put on as a coat | 10.5 |
| "why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" (2 Samuel 24:3) | a king's decision made over counsel | 10.7 |
| "the man whom the king delights to honor" (Esther 6:9) | Haman exalting himself, and his fall | Chapter 12 |
| "the king has delight in you" (1 Samuel 18:22) | Saul's snare | 10.10 |
| "If one wished to contend with him" (Job 9:3) | contending with God | 10.9 |
| "I desire to justify you" (Job 33:32) | a friend speaking to set another right | 10.10 |
| "does not wish to take his brother's wife" (Deuteronomy 25:7) | refusing a duty, and the public shame | 10.10 |
| "Whoever favors Joab" (2 Samuel 20:11) | following, past a body | 10.10 |
| "he does whatever he pleases" (Ecclesiastes 8:3) | keeping one's place before a king | 10.10 |
| "we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone" (1 Thessalonians 3:1) | sending Timothy, out of fear for them | 10.10 |
| "you will delight yourself in the Almighty" (Job 22:26) | returning to the Almighty | 10.9 |
| "Will he take delight in the Almighty?" (Job 27:10) | calling on God only in distress | 10.9 |
| "the land was pleasant" (Genesis 49:15) | bowing the shoulder to forced labour | 10.7 |
| "bread eaten in secret is pleasant" (Proverbs 9:17) | Folly's call, and turning in | 10.7 |
| "they shall hear my words, for they are pleasant" (Psalm 141:6) | praying that the heart not lean to evil, and taking a rebuke | 10.7 |
| "those who rebuke the wicked will have delight" (Proverbs 24:25) | judging without partiality | 10.8 |
| "drink deeply with delight" (Isaiah 66:11) | being comforted, as by a mother | 10.9 |
| "shall play over the hole of the cobra" (Isaiah 11:8) | creation at peace | 13.4 |
| "If the Lord delights in us" (Numbers 14:8) | not fearing, on the ground of his delight | 10.9 |
| "By this I know that you delight in me" (Psalm 41:11) | betrayed by a friend, and knowing he is not abandoned | 10.10 |
| "for he delights in him!" (Psalm 22:8) | mockery | 10.5 |
| "I have no pleasure in you" (2 Samuel 15:26) | yielding a choice to God | 10.7 |
| "if it seems good to you, I will give you its value in money" (1 Kings 21:2) | wanting another's vineyard, put as a fair offer | 10.6 |
| "Do whatever is good in your eyes" (2 Kings 10:5) | rulers giving up a choice, in fear | 10.7 |
| "Do whatever seems good to you" (1 Samuel 14:36) | a people leaving the choice to the king, the priest asking for God first | 10.7 |
| "to do with them as it seems good to you" (Esther 3:11) | a king handing a people to another's will | 10.7 |
| "you may write as you please" (Esther 8:8) | the same king handing it the other way | 10.7 |
| "If it seems good to you and from the Lord our God" (1 Chronicles 13:2) | an assembly asked to choose as one | 10.7 |
| "Let him do what seems good to him" (1 Samuel 3:18) | yielding to a judgment already spoken | 10.7 |
| "dwell where it pleases you" (Genesis 20:15) | a choice given back after a wrong | 10.7 |
| "do therefore what seems good to you" (2 Samuel 19:27) | leaving one's cause with the king | 10.10 |
| "to do his pleasure" (2 Samuel 19:18) | hurrying to serve the returning king | 10.10 |
| "do to them as you please" (Genesis 19:8) | Lot shielding his guests | 10.10 |
| "you may do to us whatever seems good to you" (1 Samuel 11:10) | words of surrender, with rescue known | 10.11 |

God's delight itself, which these verses lean on, read or throw, is in 13.1 (*Delight*).

## When feeling changes character

The same feeling is not always the same thing.
- **Anger** can heal, as Jesus's does (Mark 3:5). It can stop its ears and stone a man (Acts 7:57–58). It can be "a rage that has reached up to heaven" (2 Chronicles 28:9). "Be angry and do not sin" (Ephesians 4:26) tells me anger itself is not forbidden. What it does, and how long it stays, is the question.
- **Indignation** is the disciples' complaint at a woman's gift: "Why this waste?" (Matthew 26:8). It is also one of the fruits of a grief that turns to God: "what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal" (2 Corinthians 7:11).
- **Vexation**, *ka'as*, is what a person does to another ("her rival used to provoke her grievously", 1 Samuel 1:6), what a person bears ("I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation", 1:16), and even something that does good: "Sorrow is better than laughter, for by sadness of face the heart is made glad" (Ecclesiastes 7:3). The verse before gives the house of mourning its reason: "for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart" (7:2).
- **Fear** is forbidden and commanded, sometimes in one sentence (Exodus 20:20). The word for the fear that makes people run is the word for the fear that keeps them from turning away. The section on fear above sets out what changes it.
- **Anxiety** is rebuked when it is for my own food and clothing (Matthew 6:25), and praised when it is for the welfare of others (Philippians 2:20). It is the same Greek word. The Hebrew word for anxious dread is also the word for being sorry for sin (Psalm 38:18). The section on anxiety above sets out the difference.
- **Provoking** is what love does not do. It "is not irritable" (1 Corinthians 13:5). Yet believers are told, "let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works" (Hebrews 10:24), with the same Greek word.
- **Delight** is set on God's commandments by the man who fears him (Psalm 112:1), and on war by the peoples God scatters (Psalm 68:30). The same claim about God's delight is thanks in one psalm and a taunt in another (Psalm 18:19; 22:8). The section on delight above sets out what it is set on.

What makes the difference, as far as the verses show:
- **What, or whom, it faces.** Fear of the army and of the sea is followed, after God has acted, by fear of the Lord (Exodus 14:10, 31; the section on fear above).
- **What the feeling is for.** Is it on behalf of someone wronged, or for my own will?
- **What it is joined with.** Joined with grief, it is Jesus "grieved at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5). Joined with jealousy, it refuses every gift: "jealousy makes a man furious … He will accept no compensation" (Proverbs 6:34–35). I read grief as making it tender and jealousy as making it hard.
- **How long it stays.**
- **Whether it is seen truly.**
- **The answer it meets.** "A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (Proverbs 15:1).
- **Whether it is brought before God.** "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3). "Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent" (Psalm 4:4).

Chapter 11 (§4) sets these beside what the other activities show.

blocks.section: Remembering as a cure, and remembering as hope
blocks.text:
## Remembering as a cure, and remembering as hope

So remembering is commanded.
- **Against self-righteousness:** "Remember and do not forget how you provoked the Lord your God to wrath in the wilderness" (Deuteronomy 9:7). It comes straight after "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (9:4).
- **Against fear:** "you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt" (Deuteronomy 7:18).
- **Against the pride of having:** "You shall remember the Lord your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:18).
- **Before old age:** "Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come" (Ecclesiastes 12:1). The days that follow are pictured with trembling and terrors (12:3–5; 10.12).
- **Kept in a song**, so it will not be lost: "this song shall confront them as a witness (for it will live unforgotten in the mouths of their offspring)" (Deuteronomy 31:21).

Remembering also rescues. The psalmist fears that God's anger has shut him out: "Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" (Psalm 77:9). His answer is not a reply from heaven but an act of memory: "I will remember the deeds of the Lord; yes, I will remember your wonders of old" (77:11). The poet of Lamentations does the same in the middle of ruin. "My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me. But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases" (Lamentations 3:20–22). One remembering bows the soul down, and another lifts it.

## What thinking does

**It designs.** The verb for devising is used of the craftsmen who worked the cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1), and of people who plot. One word, *mᵊzimmāh*, covers both: "discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11), and "a man of evil devices he condemns" (Proverbs 12:2).

The same skill is put to different uses:
- The tabernacle craftsmen were given it for God's house (Exodus 35:35). Huram-abi, sent to Solomon for the temple, was trained "to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him" (2 Chronicles 2:14). His skill was to carry out a design another gave him.
- King Uzziah's engineers turned it to war: "he made machines, invented by skillful men … And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong" (2 Chronicles 26:15). The next verse: "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (26:16).
- Those "at ease in Zion" (Amos 6:1) turned it on themselves: they "like David invent for themselves instruments of music" (6:5).

**It reckons**, giving things their worth. People reckon wrongly.
- Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Genesis 38:15).
- Eli watched Hannah praying silently and "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Samuel 1:13).
- A whole people looked at the servant of the Lord and "esteemed him not … we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:3–4).
- A price can be set on a person, and called lordly in irony: "Then the Lord said to me, 'Throw it to the potter'—the lordly price at which I was priced by them" (Zechariah 11:13). It was thirty pieces of silver (11:12). Matthew reads it of the silver Judas brought back when he "changed his mind": "the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel" (Matthew 27:3, 9).
- Opponents reckon the worst: "some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh" (2 Corinthians 10:2).
- People reckon by the surface: "Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise" (Proverbs 17:28). Even a good act can be reckoned by its manner: "Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing" (27:14).
- A people at ease can be made to reckon itself: "Pass over to Calneh, and see … Are you better than these kingdoms? Or is their territory greater than your territory" (Amos 6:2), said to those "at ease in Zion" (6:1) who "put far away the day of disaster" (6:3).
- A father can reckon his own daughters as strangers. Rachel and Leah: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us" (Genesis 31:15).
- What is precious can be reckoned cheap: "The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold, how they are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands!" (Lamentations 4:2).
- When a land breaks down, regard for people goes with it: "Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man" (Isaiah 33:8). The Medes are named by what they do not value: they "have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold" (13:17), and the next verse says "they will have no mercy" (13:18).

Being reckoned is felt from the inside.
- "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psalm 44:22).
- "I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength" (Psalm 88:4). The verse before says, "my soul is full of troubles" (88:3).
- A people can reckon itself apart. Balaam, sent to curse, sees "a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!" (Numbers 23:9).
- Being reckoned trustworthy carries a charge. Nehemiah appointed treasurers "for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers" (Nehemiah 13:13).
- A man can be reckoned worthy by others and reckon himself not. The elders said of the centurion, "He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation" (Luke 7:4–5). He sent word, "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed" (7:6–7). Jesus "marveled at him" (7:9).

God reckons truly.
- Abraham "believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6).
- The nations "are accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isaiah 40:15). Yet the same God "takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17).

Jesus took the wrong reckoning on himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: 'And he was numbered with the transgressors'" (Luke 22:37). And reckoning is not mine to turn toward myself: "Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Reckoning is not only about judging. In the law it serves **release**: the man who sold himself "shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee" (Leviticus 25:50), and pay his way free. And there are times when reckoning is laid aside because there is trust: "they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money … for they dealt honestly" (2 Kings 12:15).

The Greek word carries this on. "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18). And faith is itself a reckoning: Abraham "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19). Paul says the same of Abraham before his own body: "He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" (Romans 4:19).

Reckoning from what God has done can answer a fear of dying. Manoah said, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God." His wife answered, "If the Lord had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things" (Judges 13:22–23). Chapter 2 follows the fear of dying.

**It likens.** The Hebrew *dāmāh* means both "to be like" and "to think".
- Mordecai warns Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews" (Esther 4:13).
- Worshippers say, "We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple" (Psalm 48:9).
- Love likens: "I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots" (Song of Songs 1:9).
- Comfort tries to liken, and sometimes cannot: "What can I say for you, to what compare you, O daughter of Jerusalem? What can I liken to you, that I may comfort you …? For your ruin is vast as the sea; who can heal you?" (Lamentations 2:13).

- Lament likens the self truly: "I am like a desert owl of the wilderness" (Psalm 102:6).
- God himself teaches by likening: "through the prophets gave parables" (Hosea 12:10).

Likening can go badly wrong. God says, "you thought that I was one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21). Chapter 12 follows this further.

**It murmurs.** *Hāgāh* is the word for meditating, and it is not silent. "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6). But the same word devises and plots: "their hearts devise violence" (Proverbs 24:2). And it can "meditate treachery all day long" (Psalm 38:12). Chapter 10.5 picks up its sense of uttering.

**It reasons, inside and between.** The Greek word for reasoning is used for a single heart talking to itself and for people talking together, with no change of word.
- Inside: a thought can be a whole sentence. "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 10:4). Jesus perceived "that they thus questioned within themselves" (Mark 2:8). The rich man "thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?'" (Luke 12:17).
- Between: "What were you discussing on the way?" (Mark 9:33).

**It can be troubled.** Mary "was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29). She is trying to understand. The disciples' worried reasoning about bread is different. "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?" (Mark 8:17). Jesus connects it with a hard heart and "little faith" (Matthew 16:8).

Thinking can weigh answers by their cost, not by their truth. Asked by what authority he acted, Jesus asked in return, "The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" "And they discussed it among themselves, saying, 'If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From man, we are afraid of the crowd'" (Matthew 21:25–26). They answered, "We do not know" (21:27). Both answers were weighed against what each would cost them (10.12, 10.11).

A wrong expectation can be what a teaching answers. Jesus told the parable of the nobleman and the minas "because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately" (Luke 19:11).

## Grumbling

Grumbling is complaint said out loud, by many people together, against those who lead them. The Hebrew word is *lûn*, "to grumble", and alongside it *rāgan*, "to murmur". Moses and Aaron hear it first, but Moses says it is not about them: "Your grumbling is not against us but against the Lord" (Exodus 16:8). "What are we, that you grumble against us?" (16:7). God says the same: "I have heard the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against me" (Numbers 14:27).

It starts from what is felt and what is heard.
- **Thirst and hunger.** "The people grumbled against Moses, saying, 'What shall we drink?'" (Exodus 15:24). "The people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses" (17:3).
- **A report.** The spies "made all the congregation grumble against him by bringing up a bad report about the land" (Numbers 14:36). The spies had said, "we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers" (13:33), and "the people wept that night" (14:1).
- **A death.** The day after Korah's rebellion was judged, "all the congregation … grumbled against Moses and against Aaron, saying, 'You have killed the people of the Lord'" (Numbers 16:41).
- **A promise kept.** The leaders would not attack the Gibeonites "because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the Lord … Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders" (Joshua 9:18).

What it says is a retelling of the past. The rescue from Egypt is told again as if it were a plan to kill them.
- "Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger" (Exodus 16:3).
- "Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?" (17:3).
- "Would that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or would that we had died in this wilderness!" (Numbers 14:2).
- "You murmured in your tents and said, 'Because the Lord hated us he has brought us out of the land of Egypt'" (Deuteronomy 1:27). The next verse says what was underneath: "Our brothers have made our hearts melt" (1:28).

That last grumbling was said "in your tents" (Deuteronomy 1:27; also Psalm 106:25). The psalm names what went with it: "they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise. They murmured in their tents, and did not obey the voice of the Lord" (Psalm 106:24–25). In Deuteronomy it goes with refusal: "you would not go up, but rebelled" (Deuteronomy 1:26). At Rephidim it came close to violence: "They are almost ready to stone me" (Exodus 17:4).

Grumbling is answered in more than one way.
- **With provision.** At Marah, Moses "cried to the Lord", and "the water became sweet" (Exodus 15:25).
- **With judgement.** "Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness … who have grumbled against me" (Numbers 14:29).
- **With a sign.** Aaron's staff that budded was kept "as a sign for the rebels, that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die" (Numbers 17:10).
- **With a promise.** "Those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction" (Isaiah 29:24).

One man in the crowd did not grumble, and God names what made him different: "my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me fully, I will bring into the land" (Numbers 14:24).

## Beside choosing

Wanting stands beside choosing, and the words can cross. When the king says to Barzillai "all that you desire of me I will do for you" (2 Samuel 19:38), "desire" is the Hebrew verb for choosing. Elsewhere the verses set what a person wants next to what they choose:
- **Desire:** "For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen" (Isaiah 1:29).
- **The soul's delight:** "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations" (Isaiah 66:3).
- **Envy, named before the choice it would lead to:** "Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways" (Proverbs 3:31).
- **Wanting weighed against something better:** of wisdom, "nothing you desire can compare with her" (Proverbs 3:15).

A desire still has to be carried through. Paul writes "so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it" (2 Corinthians 8:11). Section 10.7 gives the account of choosing.

A want can be met and still be refused. "David said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water to drink from the well of Bethlehem'" (2 Samuel 23:15). Three men broke through the enemy camp to bring it, "But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'" (23:16–17). His longing was real, and he set it aside for what the water had cost others. 10.7 (*Willing*) follows the will.

## Thirst answered

Twice in John people ask for the gift and mean the thing itself. The woman at the well: "Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water" (John 4:15). The crowd, who had followed Jesus "because you ate your fill of the loaves" (6:26): "Sir, give us this bread always" (6:34). Both times the answer moves from the thing to a person: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst" (6:35). The want is real, and it is not refused. It is met by coming and believing, acts toward someone, and not by a supply.

The water is pictured as a spring: "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:13–14). Jeremiah has the opposite: "they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13; Chapter 2). A cistern holds what is poured into it, and a broken one loses it. A spring wells up from within. One is a want that must be filled again and again. The other is a want met at its source, and the source is "in him".

The thirst is answered with water: "let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take the water of life without price" (Revelation 22:17). God hears the desire: "O Lord, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart" (Psalm 10:17). He gives it: "You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips" (Psalm 21:2). A desire met reaches the whole person: "a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" (Proverbs 13:12), and "A desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but to turn away from evil is an abomination to fools" (13:19). And God himself satisfies it: "You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing" (Psalm 145:16). The creatures' thirst is met the same way (13.4).

At the feast the offer is made aloud, and the water now flows outward: *"Jesus stood up and cried out, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"* John adds, *"Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive"* (John 7:37–39; Chapter 6). At the well the spring wells up *"in him"*. At the feast rivers flow *"out of his heart"*. I read a want that is met and then becomes a source for others.

The one who offered the water thirsted: *"After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), 'I thirst.'"* He was given sour wine, and then he said, *"It is finished"* (John 19:28–30). The psalm puts the thirst beside the want of comfort: *"I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink"* (Psalm 69:20–21). He says "I thirst" knowing what it fulfils. I read the want spoken, not hidden, and answered with sour wine.

The want can be aimed at righteousness, and then it is called blessed: *"Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied"* (Matthew 5:6). God's answer to plain thirst is given with its reason. *"When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the Lord will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them"* (Isaiah 41:17). *"They shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them"* (Isaiah 49:10). The end is said in nearly the same words: *"They shall hunger no more, neither thirst anymore; the sun shall not strike them, nor any scorching heat. For the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd, and he will guide them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes"* (Revelation 7:16–17). The thirst and the tears are answered together.

A thirst met can be forgotten. *"You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and brought water for them out of the rock for their thirst … But they and our fathers acted presumptuously and stiffened their neck"*; they *"were not mindful of the wonders that you performed among them"* (Nehemiah 9:15–17). Isaiah sets the same memory beside the wicked: *"They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock … There is no peace, says the Lord, for the wicked"* (Isaiah 48:21–22). I read a want met so fully that it was no longer felt, and the giver forgotten with it (10.3).

Thirst also comes as judgment, and the verses name the inner ground each time. Joyless service in plenty: *"Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joyfulness and gladness of heart, because of the abundance of all things, therefore you shall serve your enemies whom the Lord will send against you, in hunger and thirst"* (Deuteronomy 28:47–48). A choice of what he did not delight in: *"you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isaiah 65:12), so *"my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty … my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (65:13–14). The outward thirst is matched by pain of heart and a broken spirit. Drink without regard: those who *"run after strong drink"* (5:11) and *"do not regard the deeds of the Lord"* (5:12) end *"parched with thirst"*, and the lack named is knowledge: *"my people go into exile for lack of knowledge"* (Isaiah 5:13). The drinkers end thirsty.

Hunger and thirst can be borne for others. *"To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless, and we labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure"* (1 Corinthians 4:11–12). Paul's longer list ends *"in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches"* (2 Corinthians 11:27–28). The bodily wants are listed and passed over. The weight he names last is inside, and it is for others.

A bodily want can be the setting of a vision. Peter *"became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance"* (Acts 10:10), and saw a sheet let down full of animals (10:11–12). The verses do not say why it came then.

## Jealousy and envy

The jealousy words name a wanting that is turned toward what another has, or toward someone else's honour. The verses do not show one jealousy. They show several, and what distinguishes them is whose jealousy it is, and for whom or against whom it burns. The same Hebrew and Greek words are translated "zeal", and the verses on zeal are read here with the rest.

**Jealousy for another.** Elijah, in the cave at Horeb, says, "I have been very jealous for the Lord, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away" (1 Kings 19:10). After the wind, the earthquake, the fire and "the sound of a low whisper", he says it again, word for word (19:12–14). The meeting did not change how he spoke of himself. His zeal is joined, in one sentence, to standing alone and to his life being hunted. God does not argue with it. He gives him work, "Go, return on your way … you shall anoint" (19:15–16), and answers the "I only" with "Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal" (19:18). I read zeal for God that has turned into the sense of standing alone, met with work and with company.

Joshua's jealousy was for Moses. When two men prophesied in the camp, he said, "My lord Moses, stop them." Moses answered, "Are you jealous for my sake? Would that all the Lord's people were prophets, that the Lord would put his Spirit on them!" (Numbers 11:28–29). It is refused by the very person it is for. Elijah's jealousy guards God's covenant. Joshua's would keep God's gift narrow. Moses wants it given to all.

Phinehas was also jealous for God, and his jealousy turned out otherwise. *"Phinehas … has turned back my wrath from the people of Israel, in that he was jealous with my jealousy among them"*. He was given *"my covenant of peace"*, *"because he was jealous for his God and made atonement for the people of Israel"* (Numbers 25:11–13; 10.9). Phinehas's jealousy was God's own, and it stood with the people and turned the wrath from them. Elijah's ended in "I, even I only, am left". I read that the same jealousy for God can stand with the people or end in standing alone.

**Zeal that consumes the one who has it.** *"For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me"* (Psalm 69:9). The verse before says what it cost: *"I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons"* (69:8). The zeal eats the one who has it, and it draws onto him the reproach that was meant for God. Another psalm names what lights it: *"My zeal consumes me, because my foes forget your words"* (Psalm 119:139). The psalmist sets himself against them: *"I am small and despised, yet I do not forget your precepts"* (119:141). The first zeal is roused by insult to God's house, the second by the forgetting of his words. When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple, saying *"do not make my Father's house a house of trade"*, *"His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me'"* (John 2:16–17; 10.3). They understood what they saw by remembering the psalm. I read that zeal, in these verses, is not pictured as a strength the zealous one holds but as a fire that uses him up.

**Zeal for God that does not know.** Paul says of his own people, *"my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness"* (Romans 10:1–3). He knows that zeal from inside, and three times he names it as his own:
- *"so extremely zealous was I for the traditions of my fathers"* (Galatians 1:14), beside *"I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it"* (1:13)
- *"as to zeal, a persecutor of the church"* (Philippians 3:6)
- *"being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death"* (Acts 22:3–4)

Each time, zeal and persecution stand together. In Philippians the zeal is listed among his gains, and then *"whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ"* (Philippians 3:7). In Galatians what ended it was not his own correction: *"he who had set me apart before I was born, and who called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me"* (Galatians 1:15–16). And in Acts he grants his hearers the zeal he once had. I read zeal as able to be sincere and aimed at God, and still wrong, because it runs ahead of knowing. Paul meets it with his heart's desire and prayer for them, not with contempt. Such zeal can also be stirred by a report: believers *"all zealous for the law"* had *"been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses"* (Acts 21:20–21).

**Zeal put on show, and zeal that set aside an oath.** Jehu says, *"Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord"* (2 Kings 10:16). His zeal is something to be watched from his chariot. The same chapter ends on his heart: *"But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the Lord, the God of Israel, with all his heart"* (10:31; 13.1). Saul's zeal broke a sworn word: *"Although the people of Israel had sworn to spare them, Saul had sought to strike them down in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah"* (2 Samuel 21:2). The guilt outlived him. Years later there was a famine *"for three years, year after year"*, and the Lord said, *"There is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death"* (21:1). I read a zeal for one's own people that set an oath before God aside, and a guilt that came due after the zealous man was dead. Phinehas's zeal was God's own, and the wrath turned back. Saul's was for the people, and it left bloodguilt behind.

**Jealousy that is God's, in a man.** Phinehas was jealous with God's jealousy. Paul says the same of himself: *"I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ"* (2 Corinthians 11:2–3). The picture is the one God uses of himself, a husband's jealousy (13.1). Paul arranged the betrothal, and his jealousy is for the bridegroom. It comes joined to fear, and the fear is for their thoughts.

Zeal for others can be labour. Epaphras is *"always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you"* (Colossians 4:12–13). Where the ESV has "worked hard", some manuscripts have "zeal". Zeal for good is set beside the end of fear: *"Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled"* (1 Peter 3:13–14; 10.12). And it is what the redemption makes: Christ *"gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works"* (Titus 2:14).

**Envy of what the wicked have.** Psalm 73 starts with its conclusion, "Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart" (73:1). Then it tells how near the psalmist came to losing it: "But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:2–3). Envy comes in by sight, as desire does. Thinking about it wore him out until he went "into the sanctuary of God" (73:16–17; 10.4, 10.9). There the prosperity was seen again: "Like a dream when one awakes, O Lord, when you rouse yourself, you despise them as phantoms" (73:20). What he envied is a dream, and God's rousing is the waking. Then he names what envy had done to him: "When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you" (73:21–22). I read envy as a sight of another's good that embitters the soul. The psalm does not cure it with a better argument. It cures it with another seeing, in God's presence. Proverbs gives the same answer as a command, and sets it in time: "Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the Lord all the day. Surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off" (Proverbs 23:17–18). Envy looks at what the other has now. The answer looks to "a future".

Psalm 37 opens with the same pair, envy and heat: *"Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers! For they will soon fade like the grass"* (Psalm 37:1–2). "Fret" is literally *heat yourself* (10.1). The answer comes in two parts. The first is what will happen to the envied: they fade.
