**In the Son.** His majesty is received: "we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father" (2 Peter 1:16–17). His place rests on what he is: "that in everything he might be preeminent. For in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell" (Colossians 1:18–19). At the moment "all were astonished at the majesty of God", he said, "The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men" (Luke 9:43–44). Then he was mocked on that very standing: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Matthew 27:29); "Prophesy! Who is it that struck you?" (Luke 22:64); "He saved others; he cannot save himself" (Mark 15:31). He "made no answer" (Luke 23:9), and he prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" (Luke 23:34). I read that the majesty no one can overturn did not defend itself against mockery. Pride grasps a place that is not its own; he "did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped" (Philippians 2:6; *Lowering himself*, below).

# 13.4 Nature

Nature here means the creatures and the world in their own right, as the verses speak of them before God.

**God's look on what he made.** The first seeing in Scripture is God's. After each work, "God saw that it was good": the sea creatures and the birds (Genesis 1:21), the beasts of the earth (1:25). At the end, "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (1:31). His look approves what he made before anything in it has done anything. The next look in the story, the woman's at the tree, uses the same words and goes another way (10.6, *Through the eye*).

**The creatures' thirst and hunger met.** "You make springs gush forth in the valleys; they flow between the hills; they give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst" (Psalm 104:10–11). The same list runs on without a break to people: "wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man's heart" (104:15). Then it gathers them together: "These all look to you, to give them their food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it up; when you open your hand, they are filled with good things" (104:27–28). The creatures' need and a man's heart are met by one open hand. Psalm 145:16 says the same: "you satisfy the desire of every living thing" (10.6).

When the water fails, the creatures are pictured turning to God: *"Even the beasts of the field pant for you because the water brooks are dried up"* (Joel 1:20). The same verb is used of the sun: it *"hastens to the place where it rises"* (Ecclesiastes 1:5), and of a person panting for God's commandments (Psalm 119:131; 10.6).

The psalmist also takes the creature's thirst as the picture of his own: "As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God" (Psalm 42:1; Chapter 5). The difference is in what is thirsted for. The donkey's thirst is met by water. The psalmist's thirst is for God himself.

**A creature without understanding.** God shows Job the ostrich: "For she leaves her eggs to the earth and lets them be warmed on the ground, forgetting that a foot may crush them … She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers … because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding" (Job 39:14–17). Wisdom and understanding, which are inner words when they are used of people, are named here as things God gave or withheld in a creature.

**Willing.** "Is the wild ox willing to serve you?" (Job 39:9; 13.1, *Willing*).

**Harm ended.** "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat" (Isaiah 11:6). "The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea" (11:8–9). The act is creation at peace. The child's play over the cobra's hole shows it: where there is no harm, a child plays without fear. The verse gives the ground, the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord.

**Lights that rule.** "And God made the two great lights — the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night — and the stars" (Genesis 1:16). The psalm gives the same with its refrain: "the sun to rule over the day, for his steadfast love endures forever; the moon and stars to rule over the night, for his steadfast love endures forever" (Psalm 136:8–9).

**Creatures under man's dominion.** "And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth" (Genesis 1:26). "You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field" (Psalm 8:6–7). The creatures are given under man by the one who made them both (Chapter 11, section 7).

*Verses are gathered here as each part of the study is taken up again (see 13 "Other beings").*

blocks.section: A new heart and a new spirit
blocks.text:
## A new heart and a new spirit

The central promise comes through Ezekiel, twice, almost word for word:

> "And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes and be careful to obey my rules." (Ezekiel 36:26–27; compare 11:19–20)

Heart, spirit and flesh are all named, and they are renewed **together**. Stone is taken out and flesh put in. And God's own Spirit is put within, and the result is a changed life: "cause you to walk".

The same prophet also speaks of it as something people must do: "make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 18:31). Scripture holds both together. The new heart is God's gift, and it is also what I am called to take up.

David prays for it: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me" (Psalm 51:10). "Take not your Holy Spirit from me" (51:11). "Uphold me with a willing spirit" (51:12).
